pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: Urine darkening to a deep port-wine color after light exposure, triggered by carbohydrate restriction and CYP-inducing sulfonamide antibiotics, which worsened catastrophically upon administration of phenytoin. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant metabolic disorder caused by a partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD/HMBS) in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Starvation (ketogenic diet) and enzyme-inducing medications (sulfonamides, phenytoin) strongly upregulate hepatic ALAS1 via PGC-1alpha. Due to the enzymatic bottleneck at PBGD, intermediate heme precursors delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) accumulate massively. ALA is neurotoxic, causing autonomic storming (hypertension, tachycardia, agonizing abdominal pain without peritonitis), central nervous system disruption (seizures, hallucinations, SIADH-induced hyponatremia), and motor axonopathy resembling Guillain-Barré syndrome. Phenytoin is a potent hepatic inducer that drastically exacerbates the crisis. Confirmatory testing shows markedly elevated urine and serum PBG and ALA; emergency therapy relies on intravenous hemin and high-concentration glucose infusion to suppress ALAS1 transcription.
